analysis.title: GS Financials & REITs Sector Specialist: Quick thoughts into week 3 of earnings (25 Oct 2026)
key_insights: Financials had another choppy week and outperformed the market, but the mood did not match the relative performance. The desk names three primary drivers: hedge fund specialist positioning, macro/rates, and sentiment toward AI-driven growth and activity. Earnings were not among them, which frustrated fundamental investors.

A barbell of high-quality defensives (P&C insurance, card networks, senior housing REITs) and cheap/value risk-on groups (regional banks, capital-light payments, lodging REITs, life insurance) continued to outperform. Life insurance began to lag late in the week as credit spreads and investment portfolios came back into focus.

A large move lower in rates during the week was a catalyst for a broad-based rally in REITs. Earnings generally included 'higher rate related' pauses or slowdowns in activity, with some exceptions. The desk says this was generally in line with buyside expectations, per feedback.

Most debated earnings stocks last week: CBRE (the size of its underperformance was debated against the BOE surprise guide-down) and ZION (near-term NII trends versus upside to guidance, 'can you get there').

Feedback tilted bullish and the stock worked for MSCI (risk/return after the pop is now debated) and KRC. BX performed opposite to the majority of feedback. Feedback tilted bearish and performance aligned for SYF, AXP, FLG and FR.

Other inbound topics: credit spreads and AI at life insurers, Tower/SPCX as a possible upside opportunity, mortgage insurers shrugging off a potential regulatory overhang (front book versus back book actions matter), what 'fixes' the banks, pockets of consumer credit weakness (SLM -11% at earnings), datacenter REITs separating noise from fundamentals, and FICO pricing news out Friday after the close.
Card networks V and MA both screen long (V = 8, MA = 9). Inbound questions are starting to ask what happens if Visa gives a high-single-digit guide.
AXP's September spend number surprised, and inbounds wondered why they potentially saw a deceleration.
HIG: potential for additional reserve action in General Liability and Commercial Auto, and the trajectory of the disability loss ratio is being watched.

Insurance brokers: AJG and BRO charts look to be approaching an inflection point (break higher or top out). Bulls say core organic growth is bottoming but the stocks have run. Open questions: whether in-line retail is enough at BRO, whether WTW's strong R&B organic growth continues and its margin can deliver the roughly 100bps average annual gain expected, whether RYAN estimates are in a good place, and whether AJG shows no more incremental weakness versus its mid-quarter update.

LPLA: investors want any change in tone or detail on the switch to a platform fee model. Some bears use the cash flow statement to size the cost of more aggressive recruiting and net new assets. Retail brokers have active long/short dispersion trading with LPLA on the relative long side.
AMP: clarity on margin trajectory and growth algorithm is the investor focus. COIN: the question is whether crypto trading businesses and their earnings estimates are inflecting.

Lab REITs: investors want an update on demand, the disposition environment and tenant health (smaller biotechs) as rates move higher. Senior housing REITs: potential for softness in occupancy and same-store revenue, and any signs of more competition.
Credit alternatives (ARES, OWL etc.): investors want to know whether they are leaning in and deploying dry powder as spreads widen, and what they see in datacenter financing.
Boutique investment banks (EVR etc.): sentiment is low, but special situations specialist Peter Davis notes a modest pickup in sponsor M&A activity over the past week.

Chart commentary: MS is -21% from its highs and -16% since end of August while next-year earnings estimates are flat. Feedback is that bank stocks may have peaked and are closer to late cycle than mid cycle. Across big banks there is more focus on capital and on how much excess remains versus peers.
CBRE is at a trough multiple, though not at 'floor earnings' per Julien/GIR's 'trough on trough' analysis.
